subject: art-design
title: Schemes & Harmony
welcome_lead: Pick colour combinations that work every time.
meta_desc: KS3 colour theory: complementary, analogous, triadic schemes.
final_note: Use a scheme to keep your palette controlled.

concepts.def: Three colours evenly spaced on wheel.
Tints and shades of one colour.
Colour plus the two beside its opposite.
Set of colours chosen for an artwork.

walkthroughs.body_html: Complementary pairs (red-green, blue-orange, yellow-purple) create maximum contrast. Use one as the main colour and the other as a small accent.
A triadic scheme picks three colours an equal distance apart. Red-yellow-blue is the boldest. Comic books often use triadic palettes.
Analogous (yellow + yellow-green + green) feels harmonious and natural. Monochromatic sticks to one hue and varies the lightness — perfect for a calm, unified look.

mcqs.q: Why is understanding patronage important for studying historical art?
options: Artists worked freely - patronage was irrelevant to the artwork.
Patrons commissioned art for specific purposes, shaping content and form.
Patrons painted the works themselves.
It rejects all modern imagery.

mcqs.q: What did Pollock mean by his drip paintings being 'in the painting'?
options: Patrons painted the works themselves.
He painted indoor scenes.
He worked from all sides, making the act of painting central to the meaning.
He literally fell into wet paint.

mcqs.q: What attitude does Pop Art take toward consumer culture?
options: It rejects all modern imagery.
He painted indoor scenes.
It straightforwardly celebrates capitalism.
Ambiguous - it both celebrates and critiques mass media imagery.
